scenario.brief:
**Welcome to Ledgerly!** It's your first morning. Before you touch the real product, your onboarding buddy sets you up with a tiny practice folder called `my-notes` — two small files, somewhere safe to learn the ropes. This whole track runs here in your browser, so nothing you do can break anything.

**What Git is, in one line.** Git keeps a history of a folder. Each time you tell it to save, it remembers exactly what every file looked like, so you can always look back or go back. A folder that Git watches is called a **repository** ("repo" for short).

**Your first task.**

1. Tell Git your name and email. Every save is signed with them, so Git needs them once. Use: `git config --global user.name "Your Name"` and `git config --global user.email you@example.com`
2. Turn the folder into a repository with `git init`. You are already inside it.
3. Ask Git how things look with `git status`. It will say the files are "untracked" — that just means Git can see them but isn't saving them yet. That's expected; saving comes next lab.

**Two words you'll meet.** *Repository*: a folder with Git history. *Untracked*: a file Git hasn't been told to save yet.
scenario.whyItMatters: Every project at Ledgerly — and at every company — lives in a repository, and every change is signed with a name. These two commands are the very first thing engineers run on a new machine. You're doing exactly what a real first day looks like.

steps.content:
# My notes

Things I am learning about Git.

# To do

- Learn what a commit is
- Save my first change

objectives.title: Tell Git your name and email
objectives.description: Use --global so it applies to every repository on this computer.
hints: Git stores your identity in a settings file. The command is `git config`. You need to set two values: `user.name` and `user.email`.
Quotes keep a name with a space together. Email needs no quotes. The `--global` part means: for every repository on this machine.

Type these two lines, one at a time:
`git config --global user.name "Sam Okafor"`
`git config --global user.email sam@example.com`

objectives.title: Turn the my-notes folder into a repository
hints: One command turns the current folder into a repository. You are already inside `~/my-notes` (the prompt shows it).
`git init` creates a hidden folder called `.git` where Git keeps the history. You never edit that folder by hand.

objectives.title: Check the repository with git status
objectives.description: Run it at least once. You should see notes.md and todo.md listed as untracked.
hints: `git status` is the command you will type most in your life. It never changes anything; it only reports.
Read the output: "No commits yet" means nothing is saved. "Untracked files" lists files Git is not watching yet.

debrief.summary: You introduced yourself to Git, turned a plain folder into a repository, and learned to ask Git for a status report.
internals: `git config --global` wrote your name and email into a small settings file in your home folder. Every save (commit) you make from now on carries that signature.
`git init` created a hidden `.git` folder inside `my-notes`. That folder is the whole history: empty for now.
`git status` compared the files in the folder with the history and reported that both files are untracked, meaning Git sees them but is not saving them yet.

keyCommands.note: Once per computer. Use your real name.
Ask Git what it sees. Safe to run any time.

commonMistakes: Running `git init` in the wrong folder, for example your whole home folder.
Forgetting the quotes around a name with a space.
Expecting `git init` to save the files. It only starts watching; saving is a separate step.
debrief.atWork: On your first day at any company, you set your identity and clone or create a repository before anything else. You just did the first two steps.
debrief.interview: "What does git init do?" Answer: it creates the hidden .git folder that stores the history. Nothing is saved until you commit.
